title: Perfusion: fixative everywhere at once
objective: Explain why transcardial perfusion fixes tissue better than immersion for whole organs.

steps.title: Use the plumbing that's already there
steps.body: To fix a whole brain evenly, dropping it in PFA isn't enough — the outside fixes hours before the core. **[[perfusion|Transcardial perfusion]]** pushes fixative through the animal's own blood vessels: first cold PBS to flush out blood, then PFA, reaching every capillary — brain, **[[DRG]]**, **[[colon]]** — at once.

visual.alt: Schematic of the heart with vessels to the brain, a DRG beside the spinal cord, and the colon. Blood fills the vessels and a needle goes into the left ventricle; the right atrium is cut and, as PBS from bottle 1 flushes the blood out, fluid drains from the cut; then PFA from bottle 2 fills the same vessels and the brain, DRG and colon end up fixed (hatched).
visual.caption: PBS clears the blood first, then PFA fixes every organ through the clean vessels at once.

steps.prompt: Order the steps of transcardial perfusion.
items: Open the chest and place the needle in the left ventricle
Cut the right atrium so the fluid has an outflow
Flush with cold PBS to clear blood
steps.explanation: Cutting the right atrium gives the perfusate somewhere to drain; PBS first clears blood (which clots and autofluoresces); PFA second fixes the now-clean vasculature and tissue.

steps.prompt: Why flush with PBS *before* the PFA?
options: It clears blood, which otherwise clots and autofluoresces later
PBS fixes tissue faster and more evenly than PFA ever could
PFA on its own cannot flow through intact blood vessels
It permanently stains red blood cells so they can be counted
steps.explanation: Blood left in vessels clots (blocking PFA) and adds **[[autofluorescence]]** later. PBS clears it first.

variants.setup: Someone skips the PBS flush and perfuses straight with PFA.
options: Trapped, clotted blood blocks fixative and adds autofluorescence
The tissue ends up fixing faster and much more cleanly
Nothing goes wrong, since the flush is an optional extra step
variants.reveal: Clotted blood blocks capillaries and fluoresces, so patches fix poorly and the background is noisy.

steps.setup: You immersion-fix a whole, intact mouse liver instead of perfusing it.
steps.prompt: What do you predict about fixation across the organ?
options: Uniform fixation throughout the whole organ
The surface fixes well but the core is poorly preserved
Only the core fixes; the surface is untouched
steps.reveal: PFA diffuses slowly from the surface inward, so a thick organ's core degrades before fixative arrives. Perfusion (or thin slices) solves this.

variants.prompt: Immersion-fixing a whole thick organ tends to give what?
variants.explanation: Diffusion is slow; the core degrades before PFA reaches it.

sources.note: Uses perfusion-fixed and whole-mount tissue to map colon DRG endings.

reviewNotes: Perfusion logic; ties to whole-organ work in the lab.
